1 
Circumcision as a critical test case for the value of religious bioethics: 
a close examination of the writings of Rabbi Elliot N. Dorff 
 
Max Buckler1 and Brian D. Earp2 
 
1. Independent Scholar, Hong Kong 
 
2. Centre for Biomedical Ethics, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of 
Singapore, Singapore; and Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Abstract  
 
This essay examines the role of religion in bioethics through the lens of male circumcision, 
focusing on the work of Rabbi Elliot N. Dorff, a prominent religious bioethicist. The chapter 
analyses Dorff's distinctively religious approach to bioethics, grounded in the Jewish principle 
that "God owns the body" (GOTB). While this precept leads Dorff to generally oppose non-
voluntary, non-therapeutic body modifications, it concomitantly suggests an exception for 
penile circumcision, justified on religious grounds. The presence of this exception creates 
tensions with Dorff’s broader ethical framework, particularly regarding bodily integrity and 
autonomy. 
The chapter also explores the implications of Dorff's stance on other forms of child genital 
cutting, such as those practiced by some Islamic communities (e.g., “ritual pricking” of the vulva 
of young girls). The authors contend that Dorff faces a dilemma: opposing such practices would 
conflict with his commitment to religious pluralism, while supporting them would contradict his 
own religious precepts. How a distinctively religious approach to bioethics can best handle 
such a dilemma remains an open question. 
Ultimately, the authors call for a more robust engagement from religious bioethicists like 
Dorff on contentious issues such as child genital cutting. They argue that the topic serves as 
a crucial test case for religious ethics in bioethics, challenging thinkers to apply their principles 
consistently across different practices and belief systems. 
 
 
 
Keywords: Elliot Dorff, circumcision, ritual pricking, bodily integrity, religious bioethics, 
children’s rights 
This is a pre-print of a forthcoming book chapter. It may be cited as follows:  
 
Buckler, M., & Earp, B. D. (forthcoming). Circumcision as a critical test case for the value of 
religious bioethics: a close examination of the writings of Rabbi Elliot N. Dorff. In K. R. Smith 
(ed.), Bioethics and Religion: Exploring the Intersection. Berlin: Springer Nature. 
 
The finalized Version of Record (VOR) will be linked to as soon as it’s available.  


 
2 
Introduction 
 
Should religion be permitted a seat at the table in bioethics? For this chapter, we have been 
asked to consider how the topic of circumcision might inform a response.  
The simple answer is: Yes, of course, religion (and especially religious individuals) 
should have a seat at the table of bioethics, where bioethics is understood to be a deliberative, 
theoretical and practical inquiry into the normative dimensions of biomedicine, biotechnology, 
and related areas. Since religious people, practices, and beliefs are often implicated in these 
normative dimensions (the case of circumcision, being sometimes a religious and sometimes a 
medical procedure, is a good example of this; see Reis 2021), it is both necessary and desirable 
for bioethics and bioethicists to engage directly with the topic of religion, and with religious 
people.  
Of course, there are different views about how best to “do” bioethics, or what rules 
should govern bioethical debate and deliberation, whether about religious topics or seemingly 
more secular ones. But whatever these “rules of engagement” are, or should be, we would 
simply maintain that they must apply equally to all participants. So, while religion (and especially 
religious individuals) should certainly have a seat at the table of bioethics, the seat should be of 
the same general size and make as any other. In short, there should be no special seats for 
religious bioethicists, or for non-religious ones, or anyone else.    
In all cases, debaters should be clear about their premises and show how their 
conclusions follow. And if they aim to be persuasive, it will usually be prudent to pick premises 
that are widely shared among the interlocutors. Alternatively, it may be useful to show how 
different premises can -- when combined with certain plausible auxiliary assumptions -- get you 
to the same destination. Anyone can make a good or a bad argument. So, for example, secular 
thinkers sometimes propose weak or objectionable arguments about matters of religion or 
bioethics, and religious thinkers sometimes propose strong and compelling ones. Other times, 
it’s the other way around. And sometimes, as we’ll see, religious and non-religious philosophers 
reach similar conclusions about what should be done, or what some policy should be, albeit via 
different pathways.  
As one of us has argued, “we all have certain meta-ethical commitments (whether 
implicit or explicit, religious or otherwise) and we all have to try to convince those we disagree 
with that our meta-ethical commitments make more sense than theirs do, or do a better job of 
explaining a shared moral intuition, or whatever. That’s just ‘doing philosophy’” (Earp 2015, p. 


 
3 
865; responding to Biggar 2015). In other words, we all should strive to come to the table with 
clear argumentation, consistent positions, and a readiness to receive and respond to critique.  
In this chapter, we will examine the issue of nontherapeutic childhood circumcision 
(medically unnecessary removal of part or all of the penile foreskin of a child who is too young to 
consent) from a philosophical and bioethical perspective. Predominately, we will be concerned 
with the notion of a child’s right to bodily integrity (RBI) and how this might best be understood.  
When writing in our own voice, we will approach the topic from a secular bioethical 
perspective: that is, we will not appeal to any particular (i.e., particular to some community 
rather than widely shared) religious or metaphysical viewpoint to justify claims or arguments. In 
other words, we will do our best to proceed on the basis of public reason (Rawls 1997; Van 
Howe 2013a). However, it will also be important to know how a religious bioethicist might think 
about the notion of a child’s RBI in relation to circumcision. For it would shed light on a deeper 
question, namely: In the absence of medical necessity, when, if ever, are the religious beliefs or 
motivations of a child’s parents or guardians sufficient to justify any kind of surgical intervention 
into a child’s sexual anatomy (Van Howe 2013b; Sarajlic 2014; Möller 2017; Chambers 2018; 
for an alternative perspective, see Jacobs & Arora 2015)? 
As a test case for this line of inquiry, our focus will be on the writings and speeches of 
noted bioethicist Rabbi Elliot N. Dorff, to see how his distinctively religious approach to bioethics 
might contribute to longstanding debates about child genital cutting. We have chosen to focus 
on Rabbi Dorff because, as we are tasked with exploring the relevance of religion to bioethics, 
few better exemplify the intersection.   
As a rabbi and Jewish educator, Dorff has been hailed as the foremost bioethicist of the 
Jewish Conservative movement, and a guiding figure of Jewish bioethics writ large. Yet, Dorff 
has equally been sought by important secular ethics groups and initiatives (indeed, up to the 
national level) to provide an authoritative religious perspective on a breadth of moral issues. Of 
course, his positions, like the positions of any rabbi or educator, cannot be read as the definitive 
characterization of Jewish ethics (especially as regards the particular character of the Jewish 
religion, which is an interpretive tradition). However, he has often been viewed by secular 
bodies interested in incorporating religious perspectives into their work as a leading authority on 
Jewish religious law. According to Louis E. Newman, founding president of The Society of 
Jewish Ethics: 
 
Elliot’s reputation extends far beyond the Jewish community. His standing as one of the 
country’s leading Jewish ethicists has earned him invitations to address several national 


 
4 
commissions and bioethics task forces, including the National Bioethics Advisory 
Commission, where he has testified on human cloning and stem cell research; the 
Surgeon General’s Commission on Responsible Sexual Behavior; and the National 
Human Resources Protections Advisory Commission. He also served, in 1993, on the 
Ethics Committee of Hillary Rodham Clinton’s Health Care Task Force. In addition, Elliot 
has participated in several other collaborative projects through the American Association 
for the Advancement of Science and the Carnegie Foundation. In all these contexts, 
Elliot offers a distinctively Jewish voice, yet one capable of speaking to a diverse 
audience. And in each of these settings, he has earned a reputation for the depth of his 
learning, the respectful way he listens to others, and the incisive way he frames the key 
issues. It is no wonder that whenever people are looking for a Jewish authority on major 
moral issues, Elliot’s name rises to the top of the list. (Newman and Dorff 2024, p. xiii)  
 
Indeed, speaking generally, we, too, regard Dorff as a worthy illustration of how a 
religious ethicist can fruitfully participate in, and contribute to, bioethics as a discipline. He 
comes to the “table” with thoroughly researched and well-argued positions, and a wealth of 
knowledge about the strengths and weaknesses of competing moral systems as they relate to 
contemporary issues. Importantly, Dorff is also not shy about critiquing his own religious 
tradition; addressing moral pitfalls of various religious practices; reassessing positions based on 
new information; and identifying areas for—and pathways toward—moral progress within his 
religious community. The potential for such progress, as we will show below, may be attributed 
in large part to Dorff’s high valuation of vigorous debate.  
So, what is his position on circumcision? Seemingly, this would be a central issue on 
which Dorff, given his influence, approach, and specialized training, would be especially well-
suited to contribute. After all, circumcision of the penis—a matter of particular importance in 
traditional Jewish practice while also being customary in Islam and incidentally practiced within 
some Christian communities—falls directly at the intersection of religion, biomedicine, health, 
and sexuality.  
Curiously however, we are left to speculate on Dorff’s precise conception of the ethics of 
circumcision and of the child’s right to bodily integrity (RBI), as he has said surprisingly little 
about either. For example, in Dorff’s chapter on “Beginning of Life” issues in The Oxford 
Handbook of Jewish Ethics and Morality (2016), although he takes positions on multiple relevant 
issues including abortion and reproductive rights, genetic testing, sexual health, and more, there 
is not a single mention of circumcision. The subject is likewise absent (mentioned only in 


 
5 
passing, and not engaged with as a bioethical concern) from Dorff’s seminal three-volume 
series, Matters of Life and Death: a Jewish approach to modern medical ethics (1998), To Do 
the Right and the Good: a Jewish approach to modern social ethics (2002), and, To Love Your 
Neighbor and Yourself: a Jewish approach to modern personal ethics (2003), which are 
considered by many as canonical works of contemporary Jewish ethics.  
This is, in our view, a striking omission, not only due to the significance of circumcision in 
traditional Judaism, but also due to its being a bioethically contested US American cultural 
practice (Bedzow 2020). Without knowing Dorff’s position on this critical issue, or how it relates 
to his position on other, seemingly analogous practices, such as “ritual pricking” of the vulva for 
religious reasons (discussed below), we may be missing a crucial insight into the role of religion 
in bioethical debate. In what follows, then, we take a deeper look at the nature and strength of 
Rabbi Dorff’s distinctively religious approach to bioethics, hoping that this may serve as a 
window into the value of religious approaches to bioethics more generally. 
 
Framing our discussion: the right to bodily integrity 
 
Opponents of non-therapeutic, non-voluntary circumcision of the penis (NNC, we’ll say) typically 
argue that the practice violates—or at least, infringes—the child’s right to bodily integrity (RBI) 
(e.g., Van Howe et al. 1999). How exactly this right should be formulated is a matter of ongoing 
debate (Mazor 2013; Viens 2017; Townsend 2021; Earp 2022a; Pugh 2023; Mazor 2024), but 
arguments in this vein typically highlight the following features of NNC which it shares with other 
genital cutting practices widely viewed as problematic:  
 
(a) It targets, and concentrates surgical risk on, the sexual anatomy of a non-consenting 
person; 
(b) It removes healthy, sensitive tissue from -- and thus permanently alters -- a person’s 
genitals (i.e., their so-called “private” parts) without their permission;  
(c) It does these things without medical necessity  
 
On some views, then, whatever the child’s RBI consists of, it is the sort of thing that is 
violated -- or at least, infringed1 -- by any practice that has these features (BCBI 2019, 2024; 
 
1 Philosopher Joseph Mazor, for example, suggests that the child’s RBI may permissibly be infringed 
upon (and therefore not actually violated) in cases when a competing interest or other right may be 
argued to take priority (see Mazor 2019).   


 
6 
see also Higashi 2023). In addition to so-called “normalization” surgeries on the genitals of 
infants born with intersex traits, which are becoming increasingly controversial (Carpenter 2018; 
Ziemińska 2020; Muschialli et al. 2024), the most obvious set of practices that share these 
features with NNC are the ones that fall under heading of ‘female genital mutilation’ or ‘FGM’ as 
defined by the World Health Organization (WHO): for example, what is called FGM Type 1a 
(cutting or removal of tissue from the clitoral hood, leaving the labia and clitoral glans/body 
intact); FGM Type 2a (cutting or removal of tissue from the inner labia, without cutting or 
modifying other parts of the vulva); or FGM Type 4, which “includes all other harmful procedures 
to the female genitalia for non-medical purposes, e.g., pricking, piercing, incising, scraping and 
cauterizing the genital area” (WHO 2023). 
Importantly, the WHO definition and typology for ‘FGM’ does not apply solely to highly 
invasive forms of ritualistic cutting or modification of the vulva, such as infibulation, but also to 
forms that are, on any view, much less invasive than NNC of the penis, and which are, 
moreover, often done in the same families for similar reasons (O’Neill, et al. 2020; Shweder 
2022; Buckler 2024; Earp et al. 2024). Thus, it includes a practice known in English as ‘ritual 
pricking’ (khatna in Arabic; FGM Type 1a or 4 on the WHO typology), in which a ceremonial 
drop of blood is drawn from a young girl’s vulva, as we explore later in the chapter. According to 
the WHO, all such female genital practices, being both medically unnecessary and non-
consensual, violate the child’s RBI—that is, irrespective of the anticipated harm-level, 
irrespective of parental motivation, irrespective of whether the practice has been medicalized, 
and irrespective of any claimed benefits, whether physical or psychosocial (Van Eekert et al. 
2024). If that is correct, it might seem to follow that NNC must likewise violate a child’s RBI, 
whatever that right consists of, because it appears to meet the same basic criteria (Davis 2003, 
Van Howe 2011).  
Of course, not everyone agrees with the WHO’s position on ‘ritual pricking’—much less the 
proposed extension of this position to NNC. As proponents of (or defenders of toleration for) 
ritual pricking argue, the child’s RBI is not, in fact, violated by the practice, because it is 
insufficiently harmful (Arora & Jacobs 2016; Duivenbode & Padela 2019; Porat 2021; Shweder 
2022). Setting aside how ‘harm’ is to be understood in such cases (Van Howe 2011; Earp and 
Darby 2017), such an analysis implies that a child’s RBI is only violated by practices that, 
perhaps among other things, meet some minimal threshold of harmfulness. More generally, 
then, it is ostensibly an empirical matter (once we agree what harm is, how to measure it, and 
what the actual threshold should be) whether any given practice is in fact harmful enough to 
violate a child’s RBI.  


 
7 
On the other hand, the RBI might be an autonomy-based right, or at least a right whose ‘job’ 
is to protect (future) autonomous decision-making (Earp 2019; Bagattini 2015; Munzer 2018; 
Pugh 2023). Thus, it might entail that certain types of decisions—for example, decisions about 
whether non-therapeutic surgical risk should be concentrated on one’s sexual anatomy—should 
be left to the affected individual to make, if and when they are able to make it. According to this 
interpretation, if a person is capable of consenting to circumcision or ritual pricking, but fails to 
do so, the right is violated by the practice, irrespective of any anticipated empirical 
consequences. And similarly, this view suggests, if a person is not (yet) capable of consenting 
to a medically unnecessary genital cutting procedure, to impose the practice anyway would be 
to violate their future right to decide for themselves (i.e., it would violate the right in advance) 
(Munzer 2018; BCBI 2024; see also Darby 2013).  
We will not aim to settle such matters in this chapter (though we have argued elsewhere for 
something like the latter position: see Buckler 2023; Earp and Steinfeld 2018; Earp 2019). Our 
point is only that the bioethicist whose work we are discussing, Rabbi Elliot N. Dorff, has not 
clarified his position either way.  
Suppose he does think NNC (and perhaps also ritual pricking) infringes the child’s RBI, 
but that the state should permit such infringement if it is done for religious reasons. If so, there 
are various ways to make such an argument (e.g., Jacobs & Arora 2017), and it would be useful 
to see them made. On the other hand, suppose he does not think NNC infringes, much less 
violates, the child’s RBI. Well, then, it might be that he accepts a broadly harm-based 
formulation of the right (along with the necessary conceptual and empirical premises). Or 
perhaps he thinks that ritual pricking violates the right, but NNC does not—a possibility we 
explore below. Either way, it would be illuminating to know: What is Rabbi Dorff’s position? 
The answer to this question matters. And it is a key example of why we need religious 
bioethicists “at the table” to think our way through it. Suppose we are responsible for setting up 
a taskforce to determine policy recommendations related to the child’s RBI. Our job might be to 
determine under what, if any, conditions, a clinician should be permitted to cut a small child’s 
genitalia for non-therapeutic reasons. Now, who might we select for such a group? Would we 
benefit from Rabbi Dorff’s perspective? 
 
Dorff’s Jewish ethics 
 
Although Dorff does not explicitly write about NNC or ritual pricking in his works on ethics, we do 
have some clues about his general approach to conceptualizing bodily integrity. Dorff commonly 
describes the core foundation of Jewish bioethics as tied to the theological conception that “God 


 
8 
owns the body” (hereafter, “GOTB”). Here is how Dorff explains this precept in his chapter on 
“Beginning of Life” issues in The Oxford Handbook: 
 
A number of Judaism’s fundamental convictions affect Jewish approaches to the moral 
issues at the beginning of life. 
 
1. The body belongs to God. Unlike American secular ethics, in which each person’s 
body belongs to him or herself, Jewish classical texts assert that God, as Creator of the 
universe, owns everything in it, including our bodies. Therefore God can and does make 
certain demands of us as to how we use our bodies, demands articulated in Jewish law. 
It is as if we were renting an apartment: we have fair use of the apartment during our 
lease—and, in the biological analogue, during our lease on life—but we do not have the 
right to destroy the apartment (commit suicide) or harm it unnecessarily, because it is 
not ours. (Dorff and Crane 2013, p. 313) 
 
Now, secular liberal ethicists may balk at this suggestion as it appears on its face to be, 
far from a common starting point for discussion, a maximally dogmatic illiberal creed. For one, it 
implies that it is morally appropriate for humans to be treated as property (albeit belonging to a 
transcendent owner), and thus—on Dorff’s theological explanation—not entitled to independent, 
individual rights over their own bodies.2 The specifics of God’s “demands” on us may also be 
disturbing, as many are manifestly illiberal and at odds with widespread contemporary ethical 
norms. But perhaps even more affronting, to the secularist, is the implication that this principle 
applies not only as a guide for how individuals should treat their own bodies, but also in terms of 
how empowered agents (for example parents and medical professionals) ought to treat 
vulnerable individuals at the beginning of life (such as infants and small children) who may or 
may not grow up to share their overarching metaphysic (Earp 2022b).  
However, it is crucial to understand that Dorff is not a religious fundamentalist or legal 
positivist. He does not argue that the biblical commandments—no matter how explicitly stated in 
the text—are beyond moral evolution through human interpretation and critique. Indeed, as 
Dorff’s co-editor of the Oxford Handbook, and scholar of Jewish ethics, Jonathan K. Crane, 
notes: 
 
 
2 Dorff suggests that Jewish ethics operates through enforcement of duties (or commandments) rather 
than rights. He claims that this is a valuable mode through which to pursue ethics as it adds a active 
rather than passive impetus to behave morally (Newman and Dorff 2024, see section beginning on page 
31). 


 
9 
One could take Dorff to task, [by] saying that he (sometimes) holds a wrong faith.... Dorff 
evades this critique by turning not to claims of belief or theology but to hermeneutics. 
Hence he argues that norms bequeathed to the living must be continuously and 
communally re-evaluated in light of contemporary circumstances and sensibilities and 
thus avoid becoming “wrong” in the strong sense. This process therefore juxtaposes 
moral sensibilities and the Judaic textual tradition because, according to Dorff, they are 
neither coextensive nor coterminous. (Crane 2009, p. 151) 
 
Accordingly, Dorff acknowledges, “with the possible exception of some right-wing Orthodox 
groups, all modern Jews see the world through Enlightenment glasses, where the individual is 
the fundamental reality” (Dorff 2007, p. 33). Dorff also strongly defends the separation of church 
and state. For example, he has said that “Jewish law, [however] interpreted, should not be the 
basis of American law and neither should the stance of any other religion” (Congregation Brith 
Shalom 2022). And so, Dorff cedes priority to civil law to govern over all religions (more on this 
below).  
One of the most helpful explanations Dorff offers for engagement with his work is a 
reference he makes to Thomas Jefferson’s conception of “the public square,” in which Dorff 
claims, “the model is that you come together to determine public policy bringing with you your 
convictions, whatever they are. And the presumption is that through debate, very vigorous 
debate, that you would ultimately come to a much wiser public policy than if people came to that 
discussion pretending that they didn't have [their personal] convictions” (Glazer Institute 2013). 
Therefore, upon our assessment, Dorff uses the principle of GOTB, not as a dogma, but more 
so as a particularistic “framework” or perhaps a “state of mind” which he brings to ethics 
discourse. He uses this framework to argue for a religiously grounded general ethic but without 
an invincible conviction that any specific religious moral or traditional practice will remain 
accepted merely on the merit that his religion commands it.  
This explains why Dorff rarely if ever uses the theological notion of GOTB to defend 
controversial scriptural edicts in the modern context. Much to the contrary, Dorff’s positions have a 
marked tendency to align with the liberal mainstream, leading Dorff to take opposing conclusions to 
many of his contemporaries in Orthodox branches of Judaism. For example, Dorff interprets the 
Jewish religious tradition as functionally compatible with reproductive freedom even though many 
Orthodox authorities disagree (Dorff and Crane 2016; Eisenberg 2004). Dorff supports gender 
equality in civil and religious matters despite thousands of years of codified religious patriarchy in 
Judaism (Kimmel 2021). He supports sexual equality/freedom, and opposes domestic violence 


 
10 
(Dorff 1995), even though the bible explicitly condones many actions which would qualify as 
domestic violence under today’s standards (Karman 2022).  
More recently, Dorff has reassessed one of his previously most conservative positions, on 
so-called ‘medical aid in dying’ (MAID); while formerly categorically opposed, he has softened over 
the last few decades, in line with advancements in civil policy and pressure from religious peers 
(Dorff 2020). There is perhaps no better example of Dorff’s predilection for liberalism than his co-
authoring of an influential 2006 responsum (rabbinic ruling) which permits the ordination of openly 
gay clergy (Dorff 2006). In spite of the seemingly unambiguous decree in Leviticus 20:13 that 
(male/male) gay sex is a sin punishable by death, Dorff argues that homosexual Jews should not 
only be openly integrated within the Jewish community, but elevated to the highest positions of 
communal authority.  
Thus, Dorff’s hermeneutical approach makes space for a significantly modern liberal skew. 
On the one hand, this reflects a commendable pragmatism on Dorff’s part, as he pursues a 
theologically satisfying mode through which to balance competing commitments between parochial 
and universalist values. Yet from a secular viewpoint, it is unclear how to apply Dorff’s central 
meta-ethic that “God owns the body” to practical issues in bioethics, since (at least as presented by 
Dorff) we can never be certain whether God’s instructions (and by extension, contemporary 
religious practices) are righteous exactly as written (or as currently practiced), or outdated and 
deserving of reinterpretation, including through appropriate internal and external criticism. And 
nowhere is this more challenging than when it comes to the issue of the liberal values of bodily 
integrity and autonomy, and their interaction with the illiberal practice of NNC.  
As previously noted, Dorff has not, to our knowledge, committed to any substantive treatment 
of this intersection, especially not in his writings on bioethics. He has, however, made some brief 
comments about religious circumcision in other texts, and we will use those to analyze his 
bioethics positions involving other issues that clearly bear on bodily integrity and autonomy. As we 
will show, this analysis reveals some confounding puzzles and contradictions.  
 
Dorff on religious circumcision 
 
While the topic of circumcision is largely absent from Dorff’s works on Jewish bioethics, he has 
touched on the subject in other books3 focused on religious practice and social action. A brief but 
 
3 For example, see the section on circumcision in Jewish Choices, Jewish Voices: Body (2008), edited by 
Dorff. While he does not take a position on the controversies himself, he includes opposing perspectives 
from two other Jewish authors. Feminist Harry Brod expresses regret over circumcising his son, while 
urologist and mohel Samuel Kunin defends newborn circumcision in his essay, “Circumcision: The 
Medical Imperative Accompanying the Religious Imperative” (Dorff and Newman 2008). 


 
11 
interesting commentary on the topic can be found in his book The Way into Tikkun Olam (repairing 
the world) (2007), where he describes circumcision as one of several Jewish “parental duties.” As 
a part of the segment, Dorff touches on contemporary internal Jewish criticism of circumcision: 
 
In our own day, some Jews have questioned the wisdom of circumcising boys. The 
relevant medical associations have wavered on its medical advisability, recommending it 
during the last several decades of the twentieth century and now saying that its medical 
risks and benefits are roughly equivalent, making circumcision medically optional. 
 
The Jewish tradition, however, never advocated circumcision for medical reasons. Its 
purpose was instead religious. (Dorff 2007, p. 210) 
 
To begin with, it is interesting that Dorff’s immediate response to internal Jewish critique 
of circumcision is an appeal to non-religious medical associations (though he does not cite any 
in particular, we assume he means US groups; see Earp and Shaw 2017 for why), as if the 
permissibility of circumcision from a religious standpoint might hinge on medical advisability. It 
would be very interesting for Dorff to expand on this particular question, since the passage 
above seems to suggest that if relevant medical associations actively advised against NNC (as 
some European associations do; see Svoboda & Van Howe 2013; for a recent update, see 
Lempert et al. 2023), Dorff might be inclined to accept their recommendation. If that is the case, 
it would be a very important stance for medical associations to learn about, as some 
policymakers might currently assume that religious authorities such as Dorff would never accept 
such guidance.  
However, the more important issue raised above is the meaning and application of the 
term “medically optional.”  
The portrayal of NNC as “medically optional,” or as “medically neutral,” by certain 
medical associations has grown in prominence almost uniquely in the US context, even more so 
than it had since Dorff published the statement above. The most significant source of this type 
of claim is currently that of the American Academy of Pediatrics 2012 policy (AAP 2012), which 
(though expired since 2017) supports “parental choice” around authorizing medically 
unnecessary newborn circumcision but stops short of recommending it, exactly as Dorff 
suggests. That policy, and that position more generally, rests on the idea that circumcision 
confers potential prophylactic health benefits (e.g., a reduction in the risk of some infections) so 
as to distinguish it from other practices which could be considered “merely” cosmetic. The AAP 


 
12 
policy even claims that “the preventative health benefits outweigh the risks of the procedure” 
(AAP 2012, 585). Many therefore originally initially interpreted the 2012 policy as a positive 
endorsement of the practice on medical grounds. Upon this reading of the term, “medically 
optional” may be taken as a recommendation without a mandate. 
However, subsequent comments from the AAP policy’s authors have suggested that, 
first and foremost, the policy was intended to defend parental interests, with respect given 
predominantly to non-scientific values. The lead urologist for the policy taskforce, Dr. Andrew 
Freedman, explains in a 2016 clarification piece, these values include “religion, culture, 
aesthetic preference, familial identity, and personal experience,” and thus, “protecting this option 
[to circumcise newborns] was not an idle concern at a time when there are serious efforts in 
both the United States and Europe to ban the procedure outright” (Freedman 2016, p. 2). On 
this interpretation, the term “medically optional” appears to be better understood as a 
permission without recommendation.  
One of us has critiqued the 2012 AAP policy on both scientific and ethical grounds in 
other writings (Earp 2017; Earp and Shaw 2017). So have various other scholars and scientists 
(Frisch et al. 2013; Svoboda & Van Howe 2013; see also Van Howe 2018). However, for the 
purposes of our present argument, it is significant that Dorff rightly understands religious 
circumcision as being performed for explicitly non-therapeutic reasons. We take it to mean that 
Dorff holds that under certain conditions, permanent surgical body modification can be justified 
without medical necessity, and without the consent of the person whose body will be impacted. 
This is the standard against which we will compare Dorff’s other positions on body modification 
below. 
As to the non-medical rationales Dorff gives for circumcision (a subject which is an open 
matter of debate amongst other Jewish religious authorities), he writes: 
 
 
First, by literally inscribing a sign of God’s covenant with Israel on a man’s flesh, 
circumcision symbolizes that this covenant between God and the People Israel is 
immutable. Compare this to sealing a document in contrast to signing it: the seal 
changes the very surface of the paper, making it virtually impossible to change the 
document. 
 
Second, because circumcision changes the surface of a male’s generative organ, it 
symbolizes that this covenant is to last from generation to generation... 
 


 
13 
Third, circumcision has implications for tikkun olam as well. In graphically tying Jews to 
the covenant, circumcision symbolizes Jews’ commitment to Judaism’s moral duties at 
least as much as to its rites. These include, of course, the duties [regarding] speech, the 
poor, captives, the sick, and one’s parents and children. (Dorff 2007, p. 210-211)  
 
In summary, Dorff produces the following religious rationales for circumcision: 1) an 
aesthetic rationale (which includes irreversibility as a virtue thus requiring a change in 
morphology rather than mere surface-level marks on the skin), 2) a familial and communal 
commitment and relation, and 3) an assignment of particularistic morality, for which Dorff 
appears to suggest that altering a child’s “generative organ” will play a role. 
While we are skeptical that any such reasons are sufficient to morally justify the 
performance of a non-therapeutic surgery on a young child’s genitals (or for that matter on any 
person who is not capable of consenting), our skepticism is not the focus of this essay. Rather, 
what we are examining at present is whether Dorff can defend these arguments as permitting a 
type of practice he would endorse as a matter of principle, or if he instead views them as 
uniquely appropriate to newborn penile circumcision (perhaps especially as it is performed 
within traditional Judaism). We suspect the latter is more likely, as when we examine Dorff’s 
other positions on non-therapeutic body modifications, it seems there are some values in 
conflict. These conflicts, we believe, stem from the fact that non-voluntary body modification 
isn’t just an unusual or questionable practice by post-Enlightenment standards, but also by the 
standards of traditional Judaism (as understood and expounded upon by Dorff) as well.  
 
An internal religious exception as much as an external one? 
 
Although circumcision is viewed as foundational within most contemporary sects of Judaism, it 
is also exceptional in that the practice is not emblematic of (indeed, it is contrary to) Judaism’s 
general religious ethic on body modification. Per the biblical commandment in Leviticus 19:28, 
the Torah generally prohibits cutting or marking the body, and Jewish scholars throughout 
history have consistently interpreted this as prohibiting practices like tattooing and other 
aesthetic body modification. Some even apply this precept as requiring the body to remain intact 
after death (Dorff 1998, 238) (which is why some Orthodox authorities prohibit autopsies and 
cadaver organ donation; see Rosner 1971). Therefore, the value of leaving the body unmodified 
is not only familiar to Jewish religious authorities and traditional communities, it is an accepted 


 
14 
value within those communities and is typically given significant normative weight by the 
associated authorities.  
Thus (in line with his religious commitments), in most cases Rabbi Dorff presents the 
general Jewish ethic as negatively predisposed to non-therapeutic body modification, such as 
cosmetic surgery, tattoos, and piercings, even for consenting adults. For example, Dorff writes 
of tattoos that the rabbis of the Talmud believed “that putting permanent marks on one’s skin 
violated the divine image in which we were all created” (Dorff 1998, p. 268). 
However, in line with his apparent liberal leanings, we find that in almost all cases Dorff 
ultimately allows for (consenting, adult) individuals to choose for themselves. Despite his 
evident disapproval of such practices and endorsement of the religious prohibition as the ideal, 
he usually reasons that when a person modifies themselves, it can be tolerated religiously if 
their individual subjective values can be perceived as healthy in some meaningful way.  
Consider the following two passages, in which Dorff assesses the ethics of cosmetic 
surgery and genital piercings: 
 
[Dorff on cosmetic surgery] 
 
 
Whereas therapeutic surgery seeks to reestablish what existed before and was 
damaged, cosmetic surgery done for aesthetic reasons seeks instead to improve the 
body a person inherited … 
 
 
 
… The proper response to such [aesthetic] pressure, however, is not to undergo the 
risks of cosmetic surgery to resemble others but rather to take nonsurgical steps to gain 
a better estimation of oneself… 
 
 
… In line with this view, one might think that cosmetic surgery for aesthetic reasons 
alone should be prohibited on theological, if not legal, grounds, for it is effectively saying 
that what God gave us is not good enough. As such, it is an act of ingratitude toward 
God, a lack of appropriate appreciation of the body God gave us. (Dorff 1998, p. 271) 
 
 
[Dorff on genital piercing]  
 
In general, Jewish law prohibits injuring ourselves or others. Body piercing escapes that 
prohibition because it is done in the name of adorning, rather than injuring, oneself. If the 


 
15 
point of piercing the body is to add to one’s beauty, though, one cannot but wonder how 
many people besides the person so adorned are supposed to see the pierced genital 
areas and thus appreciate them as a mark of beauty. If it is only the person whose body 
is pierced and that person’s spouse, well and good. The Jewish value of modesty, 
though, demands that others should not be shown those areas of the body or the 
piercing or rings attached to them. (Dorff 1998, 270) 
 
The first thing to note is that, as mentioned, Dorff generally frowns upon non-therapeutic body 
modification. As should be obvious, this principle or rule conflicts with NNC in a straightforward 
way, in that NNC (a non-therapeutic body modification) is religiously mandated while other types 
of body modifications are disallowed. But in a deeper sense, this also speaks to a conflicting 
application of values. Recall the positive religious rationales Dorff applied to NNC: an 
irreversible aesthetic transformation of the body, the binding of communal affiliation, and the 
motivation (indeed, commandment) to act in a certain moral manner. The high moral value Dorff 
places on NNC stands in contrast to the amorality or immorality he assigns to other body 
modifications. Circumcision is celebrated precisely for permanently altering the natural—or as 
some might prefer, “God-given”—body while other practices with similar physical outcomes 
demonstrate “a lack of appreciation of the body God gave us” (Dorff 1998, 271). 
This suggests that the positive values applied to NNC are so exceptional that they are 
not even fit to serve as an exemplary model for other body modifications. Dorff derides movies 
and television for unduly influencing people to modify themselves. But if influencing (let alone 
“commanding”) surgical body modification is a bad thing for a cultural movement to do, then 
what does that mean when religions (which are, after all, also cultural movements; Brusa and 
Barilan 2009) do the same? And how can Dorff’s disvalue of surgical modification for the sake of 
“resembling others” be reconciled with NNC: a practice which is intended to mark male 
membership in the group collective, such that all are expected—indeed, most are forced—to 
“resemble” each other in a very specific way?  
Dorff’s comments on genital piercing are especially curious in this regard, as they seem 
to demonstrate consternation towards others who value or perform alterations of the genitals in 
particular. This is surprising since it could reasonably be assumed that if one regards a non-
therapeutic genital modification as foundational to one’s own belief system, one would be at 
least sympathetic toward others who also practice genital modifications, even if their preferred 
modification is different than one’s own. However, in the passage above, Dorff appears entirely

1 
The child’s right to bodily integrity 
Brian D. Earp 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Précis 
 
In this chapter, an infringement of bodily integrity (BI) is defined as any penetration into a bodily 
orifice, breaking of the skin, or alteration of a person’s physical form. A violation of a person’s right 
to BI is any infringement of their BI that wrongs them. An autonomous person is wronged by an 
infringement of their BI if they did not consent to it. If a person is incapable of consenting because 
they are temporarily non-autonomous – as in the case of an intoxicated adult or a pre-autonomous 
child – the infringement should be delayed until the individual becomes autonomous and can make 
their own decision. It is only when the infringement cannot be delayed without putting the person into 
a situation they would be even less likely to consent to (if they were autonomous) that the 
infringement does not wrong them. Given the seriousness of violating anyone's right to BI, and 
especially that of the most vulnerable persons, the appropriate likelihood-of-consent for proceeding 
with a BI infringement on a child is argued to be at or near the ‘medically necessary’ threshold. 
 
Introduction 
Suppose you are a healthy adult, minding your own business, and a stranger comes along and cuts you with 
a knife. Not badly – just a little slice out of your arm, let’s say – but enough to draw blood. If you did not 
consent to this, it seems obvious that this stranger has seriously wronged you. In fact, you might say you 
have a right against other people intentionally cutting you (or otherwise crossing your physical boundaries) 
without your consent, no matter how mildly. This is sometimes expressed as a right to ‘bodily integrity.’i 
Let’s say that bodily integrity (BI) refers to the physical state of being all in one piece, unbroken, 
undivided, intact. So, skin puncturing of any kind would negate this. What about borderline cases, like if I 
jam my finger in your ear? I’d have entered your bodily sphere, in some sense, and if you don’t want my 
finger there, I am most likely wronging you in some way. But it isn't clear whether I am actually infringing 
on your ‘bodily integrity’ as we have defined it. So let’s just stipulate that any intentional (or negligently 
 
This is the author’s “accepted manuscript” version of a published book chapter. This version may be cited as 
follows: 
 
Earp, B. D. (2019). The child’s right to bodily integrity. In D. Edmonds (Ed.). Ethics and the Contemporary 
World (pp. 217-235) Abingdon and New York: Routledge. Author’s copy available at 
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326671234_The_child's_right_to_bodily_integrity 
 
The book in which the final, copy-edited version of this chapter appears may be purchased here: 
https://www.routledge.com/Ethics-and-the-Contemporary-World-1st-Edition/Edmonds/p/book/9781138092051 


 
2 
accidental) penetration into a bodily orifice, breaking of the skin, or alteration of your physical form, counts 
a BI infringement. 
Now we have to draw a distinction: ‘merely’ infringing on someone’s BI is not necessarily the same 
thing as violating their right to BI. This is because not all infringements of a person’s BI wrong them, and if 
you have not wronged someone (we’ll suppose) you also have not violated their rights. So let’s go ahead and 
define a violation of a person’s right to BI as an infringement of their BI that wrongs them. 
Why should we think that not all infringements of a person’s BI wrong them? Well, suppose you 
have a sudden heart problem. You need emergency surgery or you will probably die. You are rushed to the 
hospital and, in this case, you give your consent to have your chest cut open so the surgeon can fix the 
problem: let’s assume that ‘consent’ means valid, informed consent here and for the rest of this chapter. As 
it happens, the surgeon in this scenario will have to cut you in a much more serious and invasive way than 
the stranger who sliced your arm. But since you gave your consent, she clearly does not wrong you by 
opening up your chest cavity. In other words, although she certainly infringes on your BI when she cuts you 
open, and while she also causes significant local harm in damaging certain bodily tissues, she does not violate 
your right to BI as we have defined it. 
Now, the two cases of cutting obviously differ in various ways apart from whether you gave your 
consent. In the heart problem case, for example, you need to be cut to have a decent chance of survival, and 
that is plausibly at least part of what makes the cutting permissible: that is, the local harm to specific bodily 
tissues is instrumental to, even necessary for, and above all, clearly outweighed by, the expected benefit of 
the surgery to your body as a whole. In fact, even if you couldn’t consent – because you passed out on the 
way to the hospital, let’s say – it would still be permissible under ordinary circumstances for the surgeon to 
operate to save your life. We’ll explore why that is in the following sections. But in most cases, if you are 
capable of consenting to a potential infringement of your BI and you don’t consent – and especially if you 
actively withhold your consent – then it is seriously wrong to cut you (or otherwise intrude into your bodily 
sphere).  
Underlying insight and two conditions 
What is the basic idea behind this principle? It’s rather simple. Our bodies are very precious to us (even if 
we don’t always take good care of them). In an important sense, they are part of who we are.ii They house 
our minds and our personalities and are the means by which we navigate the world and interact with others. 
They are deeply connected to how we understand ourselves, including our sexuality and gender identity.iii 
And for better or worse, they are with us to the end. You can lose virtually everything else – friends, family, 
house, job; even the clothes off your back – and still soldier on. But if your body gives out, that’s it. Unless 
you believe in souls and the like, without our bodies, we would not exist. 
Moreover, the particular state of our bodies often matters to us a great deal. We care whether we are 
healthy or sick, fat or thin, hairy or hairless, light-skinned or dark-skinned. We care whether we have scars, 
and where they are, and how they got there. In fact, meaningful concern about the state of our bodies can 
come down to the tiniest detail, sometimes in ways that are not obvious to others: the specific location of a 
favorite freckle that is deeply cherished by someone we love (for instance). Or the fullness of our beard as a 


 
3 
sign of devotion to our religion. Or a small tattoo we got in remembrance of our sister who died in the war. 
In other words, profound layers of meaning can become associated, quite intimately, with various aspects of 
our bodies, most often in ways that we alone are best positioned to appreciate. 
Given their role in anchoring such personal meanings in our lives, as well as enabling our agency, 
shaping our identity, and facilitating – or frustrating – our general well-being, it makes sense that we should 
get to decide what happens to our own bodies. How they are treated, whether or in what ways they are 
altered, what goes into them, who even gets to see or touch them. And this means that except in very odd 
circumstances (for example, we are attacking someone and they are defending themselves within reason), 
no one has a right to infringe on our bodily integrity, not even to remove a freckle. Unless, that is, one of 
two conditions holds: 
1 
we consent to the infringement (often because we judge it to be in our overall best interests); or 
2 
we can’t consent, because we are temporarily unconscious or otherwise impaired in some way, but  
 
we would consent if we were able – like in a medical emergency. 
We will come back to these two conditions throughout this chapter, and attempt to clarify why they 
matter and how to apply them. For example, what is so important about your consent in the first condition, 
and how exactly does it relate to your best interests? And for the second condition: How do you know what 
BI infringements a person ‘would’ consent to, if they are not in a position to tell you, and how certain do 
you have to be of your judgment? 
For now, it is enough to say that this general framework is pretty uncontroversial, at least when it 
comes to autonomous individuals (roughly speaking, adults). Here, ‘autonomous’ means: having the mental 
capacity to make adequately informed and reasoned decisions about important self-affecting matters, taking 
into consideration the potential long-term consequences.iv 
Bodily integrity for children 
What about non-autonomous individuals, though? Or more specifically, pre-autonomous individuals, like 
children? Here things get more complicated. This is because both of the conditions we listed in the previous 
section (for when an infringement of someone’s BI does not wrong them) are rooted in the notion of consent. 
But children, depending on their level of maturity, are not yet able to consent to a wide range of important 
actions that affect them, including potential BI infringements.v So how do they fit into this framework? 
Specifically, how can we tell if a child is wronged by a BI infringement, and therefore that their right to BI 
has been violated? 
Typically, when it comes to things that go beyond their ability to understand what is at stake and 
make their own informed decisions, children depend on their adult caretakers – most often their parents – to 
decide for them. The thinking is that parents usually love their children and sincerely want what’s best for 
them; and they also know more about their children and their particular needs than just about anybody else. 
So it makes sense that they should be the ones to decide. Of course, there are exceptions to this. Some parents 
are indifferent to their children or actively abuse them. Other parents have good intentions but still make bad 
decisions that undermine their children’s welfare. Either way, resulting traumas can last a lifetime. So it’s 


 
4 
very important to get clear about what the moral limits should be for what parents can do – or have done – 
to their children’s bodies. 
Setting exceptions aside, though, most parents do love their children, and really do want to see them 
flourish. And not just in childhood, but for the rest of their lives. So the aim should be to help them grow up, 
physically and mentally secure, so they can develop the tools necessary to think for themselves and 
eventually act on their own behalf. Accordingly, there are – or should be – increasing degrees of autonomy 
as children approach adult status, ranging from a helpless baby (almost no autonomy) to an older teenager 
(almost full autonomy, as defined by what is characteristic for adults). 
This has implications for how we should think about children’s BI. Based on what we said in the 
previous section (about the importance of getting to decide for ourselves what happens to our own bodies), 
it means that there should be shifting priorities for how we treat children’s bodies, depending on where on 
the spectrum of autonomy they are. Specifically, the more helpless a child is, the more it needs protection 
from BI infringements that are not clearly in its best interests, whereas the more autonomous a child is, the 
more it needs authority over what happens to its own body – both in a positive sense (what to do with its 
body), and a negative sense (what to keep from happening to its body). In both cases, the goal is to avoid BI 
infringements during childhood that would limit the child’s ability, in the future, to make important decisions 
about their own BI as informed by their ever-maturing preferences and values.vi 
Autonomy and consent 
This is where consent comes in, and why it is so important. Just think of your own case. Consent is what lets 
you decide about something that will primarily affect your own embodied self, typically based on what you 
take to be in your best interests. But you might also decide to do something that is plausibly not in your best 
interests, such as donating one of your kidneys to a sibling. Either way, though, the choice should be yours. 
We would not want to live in a world where others had a right to interfere with our bodies based on what 
they thought was in our best interests, without first asking our permission. This is why consent, rather than 
best interests, is built into the two conditions from before for when someone can infringe on your BI without 
wronging you, and so avoid violating your right to BI: (1) you consent to the infringement, or (2) you can’t 
consent, because you are temporarily non-autonomous (TNA), but you would consent if you were able. 
We have already seen that children, especially very young children (like toddlers and babies) are not 
capable of consenting to all sorts of things, including potential BI infringements. So for them, the first 
condition doesn’t seem to do much good. What about the second condition? This one seems more promising. 
In particular, it invites us to think of children, depending on where they are on the autonomy spectrum, as 
being more or less TNA. According to this picture, older children and teenagers are TNA for a shorter stretch 
of time, whereas younger children and babies are TNA for a longer stretch of time. But in both cases, the 
relative lack of autonomy is temporary, barring some tragedy or abnormality. 
Now, there is an important caveat here. And that is that no child is non-autonomous with respect to 
decisions that match – or fall within – their level of autonomy. Remember that we defined autonomy as 
simply ‘having the mental capacity to make adequately informed and reasoned decisions about important 
self-affecting matters, taking into consideration the potential long-term consequences.’ In other words, 


 
5 
having the capacity to consent. Depending on what the proposed BI infringement is, then, children will 
sometimes be able to consent – or withhold their consent – to a proposed alteration of their bodies in a way 
that is appropriate for their developmental stage. Presumably most 15-year-olds, for instance, will be entirely 
capable of making an informed decision about whether or not they want to get their ears pierced or have 
cosmetic orthodontia wired onto their teeth; and if they do not want either of those things done, to simply 
force it on them against their will would wrong them, and therefore violate their right to BI. 
What, then, about proposed infringements that go beyond a child’s capacity to give their own 
consent? Here we can turn to the second half of condition (2), which refers to what a person ‘would’ consent 
to if they were able. But how do you know what someone would consent to, if they are not in a position to 
tell you? Someone who is unconscious, for example, like when you passed out on the way to the hospital in 
our thought experiment? Or more to the point for this chapter, someone who is pre-autonomous, like a child? 
You can make an educated guess, of course; but you can’t really know unless the person tells you. So 
in most situations, the surest way to avoid violating someone's right to BI is simply to wait. Wait, that is, 
until they are no longer unconscious, or pre-autonomous, or otherwise TNA, so they can assess the situation 
and any relevant trade-offs in light of their own considered values, and then consent to the infringement, or 
withhold their consent, on their own terms and on their own behalf. 
This point should not be taken lightly. Sometimes, you think you know what a person would want 
for their body, but you turn out to be very wrong. For example, you might think that someone would want 
to be touched sexually, though they are temporarily impaired (perhaps from too much drinking). And you 
might even be right that, if they could consent, that is what they would want. But what if you are wrong? 
Because the potential harms, emotional and otherwise, that are often associated with unwanted sexual contact 
are so profound, if there is any doubt at all about the other person’s consent – much less their capacity to 
consent – it is very wrong to touch them. Now just extend this lesson to the whole range of possible 
infringements on a person’s BI that have the potential to cause harm or resentment.vii 
As we saw with the cherished freckle in an earlier section, even seemingly ‘trivial’ aspects of a 
person’s body may have great value or meaning for them, in ways that only they can understand. In such 
cases, it could seriously harm the person if those aspects were changed without their permission. So, if you 
are thinking about infringing someone’s BI who is not currently capable of consenting to the infringement, 
and you can wait for them to become autonomous without putting them in a situation they would be even 
less likely to consent to, you should. 
Judging for others 
How can you know if failing to infringe on someone's BI while they are TNA would put them in a situation 
they would be even less likely to consent to, if they were autonomous, than the proposed BI infringement 
itself?  
There are easier and harder cases. On the easiest end of the spectrum are things like feeding and 
washing a child who cannot yet manage those tasks on their own, as well as giving them required 
vaccinations, all of which preserve their future bodily autonomy with minimal interference. There are also 
‘medically necessary’ interventions for any TNA person, like the open heart surgery we imagined at the 


 
6 
beginning. For a quick definition, these are interventions that are needed to alter a bodily state, where the 
bodily state in and of itself poses a serious and immediate threat to the person’s well-being, and the 
intervention is the least harmful way of changing the bodily state to one that substantially alleviates the 
threat. These cases are easy because nearly everyone would consent to having their BI infringed if it was 
necessary to save their life, preserve their future bodily autonomy, or otherwise reliably promote their well-
being to a similarly high degree. 
When a BI infringement is almost universally regarded as something that promotes well-being in this 
way, and when judgements to that effect are likely to remain stable over the course of a person’s lifetime 
despite plausible changes in circumstance or perspective, the chance it will wrong the person, and therefore 
violate their right to BI, is very small. The less universally a BI infringement is regarded as something that 
promotes well-being, or when judgements to that effect are not as robust against changes in circumstance or 
perspective, the greater the chance it will violate the person's right.viii 
There are various ways a BI infringement could come to be widely – and robustly – regarded as an 
overall well-being promoter. But a major way is to have its expected benefits rooted in norms or values that 
are relatively fixed across cultures and times: values like preserving core bodily functions or avoiding 
premature death, for example, when there is no other feasible way to achieve those ends in a less harmful 
way. Where things get more difficult is in cases where the very status of a BI infringement as an overall well-
being promoter (versus diminisher) depends on relatively unstable, contested, or parochial norms or values, 
or when its intended benefits could be feasibly achieved in a less harmful way: for example, a way that didn’t 
involve a BI infringement. 
The main examples in this category are what are sometimes called ‘cultural’ surgeries, or other 
socially driven body modifications that are not strictly medically necessary. Things like breast implantation,ix 
traditional body scarification or tattooing,x partial finger amputation,xi ritual tooth extraction,xii non-
therapeutic male circumcision,xiii and female genital cutting of various kinds.xiv In these cases, there is no 
life-threatening illness to treat or physical function to restore. Almost no one would claim that the current 
bodily state of the person – often a child who cannot consent – poses a serious or immediate threat to their 
well-being. So why are these BI infringements carried out? 
Usually, there is a background cultural norm in the person’s group that stigmatizes the healthy body 
part in question, or that attaches perceived or intended social, aesthetic, symbolic, prophylactic, or spiritual 
benefits to its being altered or removed. Among the Dinka and Nuer people who live along the banks of the 
Nile River, for example, if a child does not have its front teeth pulled out, it may be teased or seen as 
unattractive.xv Among the Dani people of central New Guinea, if a girl does not have one of her fingers 
partially amputated after a relative dies, this may be seen as disrespectful.xvi Among practicing Jews and 
Muslims, if a boy does not have the foreskin of his penis cut off, he may be seen as physically or symbolically 
impure or as excluded from a certain relation to the divine.xvii 
A problem with these cases is that many people, both within and outside of the relevant communities, 
either do not agree that the intended benefits are actually benefits (for example, if they do not share the 
cultural or religious beliefs of the majority), or they disagree that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages, 
or they see the benefits as being based in norms that are themselves morally objectionable.xviii In cases like 
this, where there is disagreement among reasonable people about the very status of the BI infringement as 


 
7 
an overall well-being promoter versus diminisher, it is harder to predict what any given child would consent 
to if it were autonomous. And guessing incorrectly could lead to serious resentment. 
To illustrate: having a prominent scar or tattoo on your body, or missing your front teeth, the top half 
of your finger, or sensitive tissue from your penis, might be something you grow up to appreciate – if you 
strongly identify with the religion or culture of your parents, for example, or if you end up endorsing the 
relevant background norms and values. But if you grow up to dissociate from your parents’ culture or 
religion, or to reject those norms or values, you might feel harmed or even mutilated by the very same bodily 
changes.xix 
What this suggests is that parents should think twice about subjecting their children to any BI 
infringement whose status as a well-being promoter is vulnerable to such shifts in perspective. This is 
especially the case when (1) opinion among informed and reasonable people is polarized: between those 
who see the infringement as an overall benefit and those who see it as an overall harm,xx and (2) the 
infringements is irreversible. Anyone who wishes they had been subjected to a polarizing, irreversible BI 
infringement when they were TNA may have the option to undergo the infringement now that they are 
autonomous. By contrast, someone who resents that they were subjected to such an infringement when they 
were TNA has no comparable recourse: they cannot 'undo' what has already happened.  
Conclusion 
We live in an interconnected world. People from different cultures now constantly interact, and move from 
place to place, and get exposed to new ideas, and as a consequence often revise their beliefs and attitudes.xxi 
This means that the risk of wronging a child by permanently altering its body on behalf of norms or values 
that are neither universal nor stable is much greater than it may have been in the past – when people lived in 
more isolated settings and their future preferences could be more easily controlled and predicted. 
In other words, unlike the values associated with avoiding premature death or preserving core bodily 
functions (which are constant over time and shared by almost everybody), the values associated with 
particular cultural or religious practices are much less robust against possible changes in perspective over a 
lifetime. Indeed, it is increasingly common for people to adopt new cultural identities upon reaching 
adulthood, or to lose the religious beliefs they may have had as children.xxii For BI infringements that are 
based in such identities or beliefs, then, there is often a subset of affected children who grow up to feel, not 
just apathetic or mildly irritated about what was done to their bodies without their consent, but significantly 
harmed by what was done.xxiii 
This suggests that, for any BI infringement carried out on a pre-autonomous child, especially if it is 
irreversible, the degree of certainty one should have about what the child would consent to if it were 
autonomous should be very high before proceeding – at or near the ‘medically necessary’ threshold. If the 
BI infringement can be delayed until the child is sufficiently autonomous to make their own decision 
(without placing the child into a situation they would be even less likely to consent to), it should be 
delayed.xxiv

often overlap. A moral right is something that places ethical limits (or requirements) on others for how they can 
(or should) treat you, whatever the law may say. So, even if there were some country where cutting an adult without 
their consent didn’t happen to be illegal, it would still be wrong to do this because, among other reasons, it would 
violate that person’s moral right to not be assaulted. For more on the right to bodily integrity as discussed in this 
chapter, see the following references (Earp, 2017a; Fox and Thomson, 2017; Hill, 2015; Koll, 2010; Ludbrook, 
1995; Mazor, 2017, 2018). 
ii See Bermúdez (2018); Jensen and Moran (2013). 
iii See Earp and Steinfeld (2018). See also Munzer (2018). 
iv For discussion, see Owen et al. (2009).

see Earp (2015c). These discussions clarify that sex without consent is wrong not simply because of the harms, 
such as psychological trauma, that it may cause, as in some cases it does not appear to cause such harms. Nor is it 
wrong simply because it tends to cause such harms. Rather, it is wrong, first and foremost, because it infringes on 
a person’s ‘sexual integrity’ – to use Archard’s (2007) term – without their consent. In this, it denies that the person 
is worthy of respect with regard to something that is central to their personhood, namely, their ability to decide 
who may engage with their embodied sexuality under what conditions. In other words, regardless of the harms that 
may or may not follow from non-consensual sex, the sex is wrong because it is non-consensual. Similarly, non-
consensual infringements of a person’s BI are wrong, whether or not the person is harmed or goes on to feel harmed 
by the infringement. 
viii See Earp and Shaw (2017). 
ix See Chambers (2004).

Circumcision, autonomy, and public health 
 
 
Introduction 
Male circumcision refers to the partial or total removal of the penile prepuce (foreskin) (Cold 
and Taylor, 1999; Taylor et al., 1996). There is little disagreement among ethicists about the 
legitimacy of therapeutic circumcision—i.e., circumcision intended to address an extant 
pathology that has not responded to conservative treatment—nor is there much debate over 
the ethics of adult circumcision insofar as consent is fully informed (a condition that is not 
always met; Fox and Thomson, 2010; Sidler et al., 2017). What does engender controversy 
are circumcisions performed on healthy babies or young boys who are not old enough to 
provide their own consent, most commonly for sociocultural or religions reasons rather than 
out of medical necessity (Benatar and Benatar, 2003; Ben-Yami, 2013; Darby, 2015a; Davis, 
2001, 2013; DeLaet, 2009; Earp, 2013; Foddy, 2013; Fox and Thomson, 2006; Jacobs and 
Arora, 2015; Mazor, 2013; Savulescu, 2013; Svoboda et al., 2016; Ungar-Sargon, 2015; Van 
Howe, 2013). In a recent paper, Azim McMath (2015a, p. 687) argues that while much of the 
controversy surrounding such non-therapeutic circumcision stems from disputes about 
empirical matters, some of it has to do with more theoretical questions concerning the 
autonomy of the child: 
 
while still an infant, the child cannot act autonomously. Nor has he ever been able to 
do so. However, if all goes well, he will eventually develop the capacity for autonomy. 
In addition, many of the professed benefits of circumcision, such as reduced risk of 
HIV infection, will occur primarily after the child becomes autonomous. Furthermore, 
there may be alternative means of achieving similar benefits, such as the responsible 
use of condoms, which depend largely on the child’s future autonomous choices. In 
these circumstances, what does respect for autonomy require?  
 
McMath argues that while a child’s interest in future autonomy should generally be respected 
in relation to his own interests, the well-being of other parties may require that his autonomy

We do not mean to pick on McMath. In fact, his paper represents a good-faith attempt to 
navigate between the extreme and often polarized positions that have been articulated in the 
recent literature (for discussions, see Collier, 2012; Earp, 2015a). Even so, we claim, he 
adopts some of the same problematic assumptions about both the available data concerning 
health benefits and risks associated with circumcision, as well as their ethical implications, 
that have come to characterize the wider debate (Fox and Thomson, 2010). Using McMath’s 
paper as a case study, then, our present aim is to slow the reel down in order to examine some 
of the intervening steps between data analysis and practical healthcare recommendations that 
must be taken into account.  
 
Such an exercise, we hope, will have relevance not only for the debate over circumcision but 
also for other areas of health policy where there may be trade-offs between attempts at health 
promotion and respect for individuals’ autonomy. In the course of our argument, we will 
touch on some of the main ongoing ethical disagreements concerning the permissibility of 
performing non-therapeutic infant or childhood male circumcisions, particularly in light of 
conceptual questions about the nature of a child’s right to bodily integrity. First, however we 
provide some historical background in order to frame the contemporary debates. 
 
Background  
 
Male circumcision originated in prehistory as a ritual practice (Glick, 2005). It was long 
regarded by its supporters as conferring primarily symbolic, spiritual, or social benefits. 
During the Victorian period, however, doctors in Britain and the United States introduced 
circumcision not only as a measure of moral hygiene—dulling the sexual organ was thought 
to discourage childhood masturbation—but also as an intended preventive against certain 
physical diseases in adulthood (Darby, 2005). Routine circumcision reached a peak in

In the last few decades, facing increased scrutiny from legal theorists and medical ethicists as 
well as criticism from human rights advocates (Abu-Sahlieh, 1994; Boyle et al., 2000; Cruz 
et al., 2003; Denniston and Milos, 1997; Price, 1997; Sommerville, 2004), supporters of 
circumcision have sought to revive the ‘medical benefits’ narrative, casting the procedure as 
a secularly-defensible measure of individual and public health, as opposed to solely a 
religious practice (Glick, 2005; Gollaher, 2000; Miller, 2002). The search for benefits has 
been most fruitful in the United States, where, as noted, circumcision was adopted as a quasi-
medicalized cultural norm in the late nineteenth century (Gollaher, 1994; Hodges, 1997). The 
acceptance and perpetuation of the procedure by key actors within the U.S. medical 
community at that time and thereafter established the procedure as a ubiquitous birth custom, 
viewed as no more remarkable than clipping the umbilical cord after delivery. Consequently, 
the circumcised penis became the social norm (Hodges, 1997; Waldeck, 2003). There is now 
a vast literature, disproportionately generated by American doctors and researchers, 
purporting to show that circumcision is at least partially protective against a wide range of 
diseases and other problems. These range from urinary tract infections (UTIs) in early 
childhood, through sexually transmitted infections—including HIV—after sexual debut, to 
penile cancer in old age (AAP, 2012; Hodges, 1997; Wallerstein, 1980).  
 
Against this backdrop, a prominent feature of much current circumcision advocacy has been 
the underlying assumption that the biomedical evidence concerning such health benefits 
‘speaks for itself.’ Once the data are available, that is, many advocates seem to assume that 
certain medical or public health policies should follow automatically as a logical 
consequence (Schoen, 2006; Tobian and Gray, 2011; for discussion, see Earp and Darby, 
2015). This tendency has been particularly apparent in arguments that rely on evidence from 
three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) carried out in the early 2000s in Sub-Saharan 
Africa (Auvert et al., 2005; Bailey et al., 2007; Gray et al., 2007). These RCTs provided 
evidence that voluntary circumcision of adult men may reduce the risk of female-to-male 
HIV transmission in areas with high rates of such heterosexual transmission and a low 
baseline prevalence of circumcision. As Aaron T. Norton argues (Norton, 2017, p. 3), the

In light of such thinking, mass circumcision as a strategy for HIV/AIDS control is now in full 
swing throughout the African continent, with the generous backing of American funders such 
as the Bill & Melinda Gates foundation (Bell, 2015; Garenne et al., 2013; Giami et al., 2015; 
Katisi and Daniel, 2015). Moreover, it has been construed as a straightforward instance of 
applying the discoveries of modern science to human betterment, akin to vaccination 
campaigns for polio or clean water for the prevention of cholera (Bill & Melinda Gates 
Foundation, 2017; Coghlan, 2009). But the relationship between evidence of health benefits 
associated with an intervention in a particular context, and the appropriate health policy to 
pursue on the basis of that evidence, whether in the original context or elsewhere, is not 
straightforward (Cartwright, 2007, 2011). As the philosophers of science Nancy Cartwright 
and Kathryn Joyce point out (Cartwright and Joyce, 2017, p. 3): 
 
studies don’t produce policies. Rather, studies test hypotheses about whether an 
intervention will produce an effect [under certain conditions]. If the intervention 
yields a positive result—it produces the effect—in several well-conducted RCTs, we 
can say that the studies support the claim that an intervention works in the study 
settings. Now, we have a fact. But when will this fact count as evidence supporting 
use of an intervention?  
 
Answering her own question in a separate paper (Cartwright, 2011, p. 1401), Cartwright 
writes that “for policy and practice we do not need to know ‘it works somewhere.’ We need 
evidence for ‘it-will-work-for-us’ claims: the treatment will produce the desired outcome in 
our situation as implemented here.” For this, in turn, we need “a large and varied inductive 
base … lots of RCTs from different populations—plus reason to believe the observations are 
projectable, plus an account of the range across which they project.” In other words, while 
efficacy might be demonstrated under ideal/research conditions, there is no guarantee that an 
intervention will be effective in a real world setting. Thus effectiveness trials, also known as 
translational research, are typically undertaken before generalized policy positions are taken. 
No such translational research was performed in regards to male circumcision and HIV 
infection.

is, they recognize that even if the RCT findings are taken at face value, they are not sufficient 
to show that circumcision will be effective—much less prudent on public health or ethical

Unlike the identification of pre-cancerous cells in the cervix, say, that may be associated with 
an increase in the future risk of cervical cancer, “arguments that the foreskin poses a risk do 
not rely on claims that the foreskin’s cells have become compromised, but rather, on claims

Construing a healthy body part as in-and-of-itself a source of risk has proven strategically 
valuable for circumcision advocates: “if HIV susceptibility is an inherent feature of the 
foreskin, it becomes easier to dismiss contextual factors that may have shaped the RCT

It is true that human genital mucosa, whether found on the bodies of males or females, may 
be penetrated by HIV (Cold and Taylor, 1999; Hladik and Hope, 2009; Taube et al., 2007). It 
is not implausible, therefore, that reducing the surface area of such mucosa—in males, by 
excising the foreskin—would lower a person’s risk of becoming infected with HIV by some 
amount, just as excising any other body part would reduce the risk of some disease affecting 
it, or introduced to other body sites through it (Earp et al., in press; Kluge, 1994). But to slide 
from such a biological assertion to the proposition that circumcision is therefore on balance 
desirable as a personal or public health intervention is a non sequitur (Darby, 2016). There 
are many possible responses to such claims, and the appropriate response will be determined 
not by science by in and itself, but also by the relevant values of the individuals and societies 
in question (Douglas, 2009).  
 
The very notion of what constitutes optimal health, for example, is subject to cultural 
variation (Levesque and Li, 2014), and a preference for (say) a modest reduction in the 
absolute risk of a treatable infection over certain kinds of sexual sensation or experiences of 
bodily integrity is also a culturally influenced priority (Dekkers et al., 2005; Dekkers, 2009; 
Earp, 2017a, 2017b; Earp and Darby, 2017). It is telling that in countries where circumcision
